method: Flesch-Kincaid estimate with regex syllable heuristic; fragments treated as sentences. Diagnostic only.
jargonCheck: No unexplained MEL, AD, NDT, FOD or professional numeric limits. Finding brief explained before use; four everyday job terms defined with examples before practice.

sample: The First Airline Shift
Start at 50. Seven decisions change reputation by +6 or -6. Reach 85. Practice is unscored.
Before the next flight
Your first week at fictional Gannet Regional Airlines starts in its coastal maintenance hangar.
The next team needs facts
A passenger aircraft needs review. Prepare a finding brief: a short note listing concerns and unfinished work.
Sora has your first assignment
“I’m Sora, your mechanic mentor. You’ll help me observe and record concerns. I’ll review your work.”
Learn under supervision
“Use our current instructions for this aircraft and task. Trained, authorized staff decide when it can fly again.”
Caleb is setting up
Caleb, another support mechanic, brings the check packet. He hopes to earn the next training assignment.
Sora asks you to help with a visual check. Which instructions should you open first?
A procedure remembered from another aircraft
A familiar procedure may not apply to this aircraft.
Current airline instructions for this aircraft and task
The reference must match the aircraft and the assigned work.
An online clip showing a similar check
A similar-looking check does not establish the applicable procedure.
Four words on the floor
Something that needs checking. Example: a rub mark on a cable cover.
Records linking a part to its source. Example: a supplier record.
An item out of place that could cause harm. Example: a metal clipping.
Passing work and its status to another person. Example: naming an unfinished check.
Match each work situation to the term.
Reported concern
Part history
Loose debris
Handoff
You connected the terms to real work.
Use the situation and the meaning of each term.
Check four situations from the hangar.
A reported concern needs checking. A cable cover has a rub mark. Which note records what you saw?
Rub mark observed; assessment needed
That states an observation without inventing a diagnosis.
Electrical system has failed
A rub mark alone does not prove a system failure.
Part history links a part to its source. The label and paperwork differ. What should you do?
Assume a similar appearance is enough
Appearance does not resolve a documentation mismatch.
Ask the mentor to resolve the mismatch
The mismatch needs review before the part is used.
Loose debris can cause harm. Which item should you flag?
A metal clipping on the work-area floor
Loose material can become foreign object debris.
A closed, secured storage case
The secured case is in its assigned place.
A handoff shares work status. One check is unfinished. What should the next shift hear?
All checks are complete
That hides unfinished work.
Which check remains open and who reviews it next
The next team needs an accurate starting point.
You kept observations, parts records, debris, and open work clear.
Review the terms and corrections before the next hangar task.
Observe. Record. Flag.
“Describe what you see and where. Flag concerns for review. Don’t guess the cause or choose a repair.”
During Sora’s check, you see a rub mark on the left cable cover. Its cause is unknown. What do you record?
A confirmed electrical failure
You have not established an electrical failure.
Nothing, because no warning appeared
A visible concern still needs review even without a warning.
Rub mark on left cable cover; ask Sora to review
The note gives the concern and location without guessing its cause.
Elena checks the evidence
Elena, the maintenance supervisor, reviews your draft note and a replacement kit’s paperwork.
Looks are not enough
“Compare the kit label with its records. If they differ, ask for review. Don’t guess why they differ.”
Keep your authority clear
“Flag concerns for Sora. With training, you can become a technician, then a lead. Approval needs the right authority.”
Aircraft Support Mechanic
Aircraft Maintenance Technician
Lead Technician
Maintenance Supervisor
The kit label says K-42; its paperwork says K-24. Gannet rules say hold mismatched kits for review. Choose two actions.
Change the paperwork to match the kit
Put the kit in the marked hold area
Claim the supplier sent a fake part
Tell Sora: label K-42, paperwork K-24
Install it because the shape looks right
You kept the kit out of use and gave the reviewer the exact mismatch.
Keep the kit out of use and report the mismatch. Do not alter records or install it.
There is more to practice
Use the corrections as you prepare the finding brief.
Your first checks are on track
You used the instructions, recorded a concern, and kept an uncertain kit out of use.
The brief moves forward
Your draft is ready. The kit stays on hold while authorized staff review the mismatch.
Caleb wants to be noticed
Caleb returns from setup. He hopes today’s effort will earn him another supervised assignment.
Your work. His claim.
Caleb calls your finding brief his own. The saved draft history shows your work.
Caleb claims your finding brief. The draft history shows you prepared it. How should you raise the issue?
Accuse Caleb over the hangar radio
A public accusation interrupts work and escalates the conflict.
Speak privately with Sora and show the draft history
A calm private conversation gives the mentor facts without disrupting the team.
Remove Caleb’s inspection notes
Removing work harms the record the team needs.
One person is reassigned
A technician moves to another job. Your brief is due this shift. One check remains unfinished.
One check remains unfinished after a technician leaves. Your brief is due this shift. What do you message Sora?
“I’ll mark the check complete to meet the deadline.”
A deadline does not make incomplete work complete.
“I’ll take over the check without supervision.”
The assignment and supervision still belong to the qualified team.
“Can you reset priorities? I’ll list the open check and next owner.”
Sora can organize the work while your note keeps its unfinished status clear.
Facts reach the reviewer
You send Sora the brief. It lists the rub mark, kit hold, and unfinished check for review.
Priya needs a hand
Priya, a support mechanic on the next shift, asks how to record an unfinished check.
You have time to help
Your brief is submitted. Priya’s handoff is due next. She needs the open check, status, and reviewer.
Priya needs help recording an unfinished check. You have time. Rank these responses from most to least supportive.
You help your teammate while preserving the actual status and the supervisor’s role.
Direct support comes first; signing unfinished work complete comes last.
Sora notices the difference
“Clear notes help the next team. They show what still needs review and who to ask.”
First shift complete
Your brief is delivered. Authorized staff assess the concerns and decide when the aircraft can fly again.
Your first airline shift
You used current instructions, recorded concerns, checked part records, and supported the next shift.
Your clear observations gave the airline team a useful starting point.
You completed this fictional supervised airline shift.
